Open Systems within a Closed Universe

Dissipation, Flow, and Form

Organisms are open systems — they sustain order by exchanging energy, matter, and information with their environment. The universe, considered as a whole, is treated as a closed (ideally isolated) system with conserved energy and increasing entropy. Life therefore persists as local negentropy within a global trend to dispersion; it does so by dissipating energy.

System Types and Boundaries

System Exchanges Entropy Trajectory Notes
Open (Organism) Energy, matter, information Local ↓ (maintained) Requires continuous flow
Closed (Universe) Energy (internally conserved), no “outside” Global ↑ Second Law applies to the whole
Isolated (Ideal) None Entropy ↑ to maximum Theoretical limit

Thermodynamic Flow: From Star to Self

The living Earth is driven by a flux of low‑entropy solar photons. Ecosystems channel this gradient; organisms convert it into work and structure, returning high‑entropy heat to space. This is the essence of dissipative structure—order sustained by flow.

Sun → Earth → Organism → Heat → Space

Dissipation and Form (Prigogine)

Far‑from‑equilibrium systems can self‑organise: convection cells, flames, hurricanes, and living cells are patterns that exist only because they dissipate energy. The brain is such a structure—maintaining low internal entropy via continuous metabolic throughput.

Information & Memory

Entropy is also an information measure. Organisms store past corrections (memory) to anticipate and reduce surprise. Memory thus acts as temporal homeostasis—stabilising predictions while reconsolidation updates them when environments change.

Philosophical Lens

Perspective Expression
Physical “Life is ordered flow balanced by exported disorder.”
Informational “Organisms are local negentropy engines.”
Ecological “Boundaries are membranes—not walls.”
Phenomenological “Consciousness is organised energy in motion.”

Bridge to the Spine Select → Change → Reconstruct

Spine Stage Open‑System Operation Closed‑System Constraint
Select Import low‑entropy inputs Finite gradients; cost to acquire
Change Transform into structure/work Energy conservation; dissipation
Reconstruct Store as memory; export waste Entropy increase overall
